q-334180.name: Question 1
q-334180.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14247879/assets/d7f1d5de28c6479a2e9b8b33a6da25a4091b71b58f6dc0c535ef390c4cb97799.png)

If the figure above shows the graph of $g(x),$ then

${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}}=$
 {{field-1}}.
q-334180.worked_solution:
Applying the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(g(x)\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }g(x)\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the graph, we get that ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }g(x)=-2.$ Therefore, the above becomes:

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}}=-2\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})=0,
$$

we can evaluate our limit as follows:

$$
-2\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}=-2\cdot 0=0
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{g(x)}{{x}^{2}}=0.
$$

q-78081.name: Question 2
q-78081.worked_solution:
First, we use the algebra of limits to pull out the constant factor of $-7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }(-\frac{7}{{x}^{5}}) & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }(-7\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{5}}) \\  & =-7\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the fact that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}=0,
$$

$$
-7\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}=-7\cdot 0=0

q-334193.name: Question 4
q-334193.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite our limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{-4}{({x}^{2}-3)^{3}}=-4\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{({x}^{2}-3)^{3}}
$$

For any non-constant polynomial $P(x),$ we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \pm \infty }(\frac{1}{P(x)})=0.
$$

Therefore, since $({x}^{2}-3)^{3}$ is a non-constant polynomial, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{({x}^{2}-3)^{3}}=0.
$$

Finally, we can evaluate the original limit as follows:

$$
-4\cdot {lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{({x}^{2}-3)^{3}}=-4\cdot 0=0
$$

q-36453.name: Question 7
q-36453.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits,  as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{7}{3x} & =\frac{7}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the fact that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}(\frac{1}{x})=-\infty ,\,{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\frac{1}{x})=\infty .
$$

We conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{1}{x})=\text{DNE}.
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\frac{7}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x}=\text{DNE}.
$$

q-46970.name: Question 8
q-46970.worked_solution:
First, we simplify the limit:

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{9}{12{x}^{4}}={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{3}{4{x}^{4}}
$$

Then, we use the algebra of limits to pull out the constant factor of $\frac{3}{4}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{3}{4{x}^{4}} & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{3}{4}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}\end{aligned}
$$

We recall the graph of the function $y=\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14247879/assets/fa92c457186fbdf71552ec79c782af7983e6fa09009e7f0efdd02b8f74e3ab98.png)

From the graph, we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to ({0}^{+})}\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}=\infty 
$$

The positive factor of $\frac{3}{4}$ does not change the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that

$$
\frac{3}{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\frac{1}{{x}^{4}}=\infty .
$$

q-305776.worked_solution:

$$

$$

Now, we can sketch the graph of $y=\frac{1}{(x-5)^{6}}$ as follows:

1\. Take the graph of $y=\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}.$

2\. Translate it to the right by $5$ units. This gives $y=\frac{1}{(x-5)^{6}},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14247879/assets/574b270248f2acc2a2eb3403f5626e420f5f16abc6e9e01dcb147df83e5806b5.png)

From the graph, we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {5}^{-}}\frac{1}{(x-5)^{6}}=\infty .
$$

Finally, the negative factor of $-\frac{9}{4}$ changes the sign of the limit. Therefore, we conclude that

$$
-\frac{9}{4}\cdot {lim}_{x\to {5}^{-}}\frac{1}{(x-5)^{6}}=-\infty .
$$
